turns.prompt_text: On mac, in fish terminal how do I find if the firewall is on?
turns.response_html:
Since you're using Fish shell on a Mac, the command to check your firewall status isn't actually specific to the shell itself—it’s a system-level utility called socketfilterfw.

However, the path to that command is a bit of a trek, so I've broken down the quickest ways to run it and how to make it easier for next time.

The Direct Command

Copy and paste this into your terminal:

/usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getstate
  • If it's on: You’ll see Firewall is enabled. (State = 1)
  • If it's off: You’ll see Firewall is disabled. (State = 0)

Pro-Tip: Make a Fish Alias

Because no one wants to type /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/... every time, you should create a shortcut (alias) in Fish.

  1. Create the alias: 
    alias checkfirewall='/usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getstate'
  2. Save it permanently: 
    funcsave checkfirewall

Now, you can just type checkfirewall whenever you're feeling cautious.

Alternative: The "Global" Way

If you prefer using the more modern sysadminctl tool (which is easier to remember), you can run:

sysadminctl -firewallStatus

Note: This command is often more "chatty" and might require your admin password via a pop-up or sudo, depending on your macOS version and permissions.

Summary Table

GoalCommand
Check Status/usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getstate
Turn ONsudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --setglobalstate on
Turn OFFsudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --setglobalstate off

turns.prompt_text: Can I put a sub-fish config in the same folder as my functions?
turns.response_html:
Technically, you can place a .fish file in your ~/.config/fish/functions/ folder, but it won't behave like a standard configuration file.

Because of how Fish handles autoloading, there are specific rules you should know to avoid frustration.

How Fish Will Treat That File

Fish specifically looks at the functions directory to find autoloaded functions. Here is what happens if you put a config script there:

  • It won't run on startup: Fish does not source every file in the functions folder when it launches. It only sources config.fish.
  • The "Name Match" Rule: Fish only looks inside that folder when you call a command that it doesn't recognize yet. If you have a file named my_setup.fish, Fish will only source it the moment you type my_setup in your terminal.
  • Variable Scope Issues: If your sub-config defines variables (like set PATH ...), those variables might not be available until you manually "trigger" that file by calling the function name.

The Better Way: Using conf.d

If your goal is to keep your main config.fish clean by splitting it into smaller pieces, the conf.d folder is exactly what you are looking for.

  • Path: ~/.config/fish/conf.d/
  • Behavior: Fish automatically sources every .fish file in this folder at startup, in alphabetical order.
FolderPurposeLoading Behavior
functions/Individual commands/functions.Lazy loaded (only when called).
conf.d/Modular configuration/settings.Eager loaded (at shell start).

If you insist on using the functions folder...

If you truly want a "sub-config" inside functions, you would have to manually source it from your main config.fish like this:

# Inside ~/.config/fish/config.fish
source ~/.config/fish/functions/my_sub_config.fish

However, this defeats the purpose of Fish's autoloading architecture. The "best practice" is to move those configuration snippets to ~/.config/fish/conf.d/.

Are you trying to organize specific environment variables, or are you looking to keep your alias definitions separate from your main config?

turns.prompt_text: in conf.d, can I make sub-folders?
turns.response_html:
The short answer is no, not by default.

Fish is intentionally simple: it automatically sources any file ending in .fish directly inside ~/.config/fish/conf.d/, but it does not recurse into subdirectories. If you create ~/.config/fish/conf.d/work/git.fish, Fish will simply ignore it.

However, you have two main ways to handle this depending on how much "magic" you want in your config.

Option 1: The Manual Approach (Cleanest)

If you want to group related settings into a sub-folder, you can keep the folder there and tell your main config.fish to go get it.

  1. Create your folder: ~/.config/fish/conf.d/my_extra_settings/
  2. In your ~/.config/fish/config.fish, add: 
    for file in ~/.config/fish/conf.d/my_extra_settings/*.fish
    source $file
end

Option 2: Use a "Loader" Script (The Fish Way)

If you want to keep conf.d organized with folders but still want things to load automatically, you can create a single script inside conf.d that acts as a gatekeeper.

  1. Create a file at ~/.config/fish/conf.d/loader.fish.
  2. Add this logic to it: 
    # This script finds all .fish files in subdirectories of conf.d and sources them
for file in (find (status dirname) -type f -name "*.fish" -not -path (status filename))
    source $file
end

Visualizing the Fish Config Hierarchy

LocationRecursive?Loading Priority
conf.d/*.fishNoHigh (Loads at start)
functions/*.fishNoLazy (Loads when called)
completions/*.fishNoTab-triggered

Why doesn't Fish do this automatically?

Fish developers prioritize startup speed. Scanning deep directory trees every time you open a new terminal tab adds "shell lag." By keeping conf.d flat, Fish ensures that your shell prompt appears almost instantly.

A quick tip: If your conf.d is getting so messy that you need folders, it might be a sign that some of those configurations should actually be functions. If a piece of code doesn't need to run every single time you open the terminal, moving it to functions/ is better for performance.

Are you trying to separate configurations for different environments (like Work vs. Personal), or just looking to tidy up a long list of aliases?

turns.prompt_text: Okay. Starting something different in fish. I'd like to be able to toggle on and off the firewall.
turns.response_html:
Since you're working in Fish, the most "Fish-like" way to do this is to create a function that accepts an argument (like on or off). This is much cleaner than having two separate commands.

Here is a robust function you can use to toggle your macOS firewall.

1. Create the Function

Run this in your terminal to open the Fish editor:

funced firewall

2. Paste the Logic

When the editor opens, paste this code in:

function firewall --description 'Toggle macOS firewall on or off'
    set -l action $argv[1]
    set -l fw_path "/usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw"

    switch "$action"
        case on
            sudo $fw_path --setglobalstate on
        case off
            sudo $fw_path --setglobalstate off
        case status ''
            $fw_path --getstate
        case '*'
            echo "Usage: firewall [on|off|status]"
    end
end

3. Save it

Type funcsave firewall to make it permanent.

How to use it

Now your terminal has a dedicated command for the firewall:

  • Check status: firewall (or firewall status)
  • Enable: firewall on
  • Disable: firewall off

Why use switch instead of if?

In Fish, the switch statement is generally considered more readable for "command-style" functions. It allows you to easily add more cases later—for example, if you wanted to add a firewall restart or firewall report option.

Heads up: Because changing system security settings requires root access, macOS will prompt you for your sudo password (or Touch ID) whenever you run the on or off commands.

Pro-Tip: Adding Color

If you want to get fancy, you can add some color to the output so you can see the status at a glance. You can replace the status line in the function with:

set -l state ($fw_path --getstate)
if string match -q "*enabled*" "$state"
    set_color green; echo $state; set_color normal
else
    set_color red; echo $state; set_color normal
end
